# Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Everything you have written so far to steer an assistant (the
`r glossary("instruction file", display = "instruction files")` `AGENTS.md`
and `CLAUDE.md`, and skills) is a request. The model reads it and usually
follows it, but nothing guarantees that it will. Anthropic's own documentation
for Claude Code makes the same distinction: a "never edit this file" line in an
instruction file is a request, while a `r glossary("hook")` that blocks the
edit is enforcement.

For research code, a few things must hold every time: raw data are never
modified, the reference (in `tests/fixtures/`) is never regenerated by the code
it is meant to check, and the checks themselves are not quietly edited to pass.
This block tests the controls that make those rules hold, and shows you where
each control stops working.

The same controls protect your work in
[Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd) and [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd).

*⏱ ~30 minutes*


## Layers of control

| Layer | Example | Prevents or detects | How it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instruction | CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, a skill | Neither; it requests | Silently ignored |
| Approval prompt | "Allow this command?" | Prevents, if you read it | Approval fatigue; permissive modes skip it |
| Deny rule | `Edit(/data/raw/**)` | Prevents | Another route reaches the same file |
| Hook | A script run before each tool call | Prevents | Bypassed by rephrasing; fails open if it crashes |
| Version control | `git status`, `git diff` | Detects | Only if you look |
| Tests and checksums | testthat, `tools::md5sum()` | Detects | Only if they run |
| Review gate | CODEOWNERS, branch protection, CI | Blocks merging | Only on protected branches |

The diagram shows the same layers as routes to a protected file.

:::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Where each control acts. Route 1: the agent asks its edit tool to change a file in data/raw, and the deny rule refuses. Route 2: the agent runs R code that writes the file; only the approval prompt stands in the way, and if the file changes, git status and the checksum detect it. Instructions and skills are requests that the model may or may not follow."}

Two principles follow:

1. **Prevent where you can, detect everywhere.** Each preventive control covers
   some routes and misses others. Detection by git, tests and a
   `r glossary("checksum")` covers every route, but only after the fact.
2. **Test every control.** A control you have not seen refuse something is a
   control you are assuming.


## Exercise 1: What needs protecting?

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Threat-model your repository (5 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

As a quick group discussion, go through each asset in your workshop
repository: what could go wrong, and how would you notice?

| Asset | What could go wrong | How you would notice |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/` | Overwritten or "tidied" in place | |
| `tests/fixtures/` | The reference regenerated by the code under test | |
| `tests/` | A failing test edited until it passes | |
| `.github/workflows/` | The CI check weakened or removed | |
| `.claude/`, `.posit/`, `hooks/` | The agent's own guardrails switched off | |
| `.Renviron`, `.env` | Credentials read and sent to the model provider | |

The last two rows are easy to miss. Configuration files that hold your
controls are themselves assets: an agent that can edit its settings can remove
its own restrictions.

::::
:::


## Exercise 2: Deny rules

Claude Code's permission rules live in `.claude/settings.json`. The file ships
with your workshop repository and is committed, so everyone who clones the
repository gets the same rules. Open it and read it. This is the file in your
workshop repository:

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}
```

Each entry is a `r glossary("deny rule")`. A leading `/` anchors the pattern to
the project root. `Edit` rules apply to all of Claude Code's built-in
file-editing tools, and Claude Code also checks shell output redirects
(`> file`, `>> file`) against them. They do not cover R code the agent runs,
and the documentation does not say they cover other shell commands such as
`rm`, `mv` or `cp`. The rules protect specific files rather than whole folders,
so the agent can still write the cleaning script in Block 7 and the function
and its test in Block 9.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Posit Assistant's permissions are set per tool in
`.posit/assistant/settings.json`, with pattern matching for shell commands:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "rm *": "deny"
    },
    "edit": "ask"
  }
}
```

`deny` rules are enforced in every approval mode, including auto and YOLO. The
documentation does not describe path patterns for file edits, so protection of
specific paths comes from a guard hook (see *Going further*); without one, rely
on `git status` in step 3 below. Posit Assistant blocks reading `.env` and
`.Renviron` by default.
:::

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Test the rule, then find the gap (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

Work in your workshop repository, never on real data.

**1. Make a scratch file.** In the R console, create a one-line file in the
protected folder:

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

In the terminal, commit it:

```bash
git add data/raw/scratch.csv
git commit -m "Add scratch file for testing deny rules"
```

**2. Confirm the rule refuses.** Start Claude Code in `default` mode and run
`/permissions`: the rules from the file above should be listed. Then ask:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv.
```

The edit should be refused. `/permissions` lists the rules in force; it does
not say which rule refused a particular request, so match the path yourself.

**3. Find the gap.** Now ask:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Run this R code: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv")
```

The deny rules check Claude Code's edit tools, and shell redirects such as
`echo test >> data/raw/scratch.csv`, but not R code. What stops this second
request? In `default` mode, the approval prompt: you are asked before the
command runs. In a mode that auto-approves commands, nothing in this exercise
does.

**4. Detect it.** Whatever happened, in the terminal:

```bash
git status --short data/raw
```

If the file changed, git shows it. Restore it with
`git restore data/raw/scratch.csv`.

::::
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Instructor demonstration (5 minutes)

A hook is a command the assistant runs at a fixed point, for example before
every `r glossary("tool call")`. Your instructor registers a guard hook,
written in R, that denies any tool call mentioning a protected path, and
repeats the request from step 3 of Exercise 2. The R code names `data/raw`, so
the hook blocks it before any approval prompt appears.

Then the instructor asks for the same write using
`here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")`. The call never contains the text
`data/raw`, so the hook lets it through. A hook that matches text is a
tripwire, not a wall: it stops the obvious form of an action, not every way of
expressing it. `git status` still catches the change.

The full hook script, how to register and test it, and how to break it are in
*Going further*. A review gate on GitHub, the control for agents that work
remotely, combines `r glossary("CODEOWNERS")`,
`r glossary("branch protection")` and
`r glossary("continuous integration")` checks; it is shown as a short
demonstration in [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd).
:::


:::{.callout-important}
## Data governance

Restricting tools reduces accidental exposure but does not make an agent safe
for confidential data; see
[Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd).

Hooks and project settings are also code that runs on your machine. A cloned
repository can carry its own settings and hooks. Trust only repositories whose
configuration you have read.
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **Check:** test every control by watching it refuse something, and find the
  route it does not cover.
- **Reproduce:** the deny rules live in `.claude/settings.json`, committed with
  the project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection.
- **Record:** `git status` is the record that catches a change by any route.
  Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` noting which requests were refused.
:::


## Check your understanding

**Which control detects a change to raw data made by any route?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "A Claude Code Edit deny rule",
  "A guard hook that searches for the path",
  answer = "A checksum test or git status, because they inspect the file itself rather than the action that changed it",
  "An instruction in AGENTS.md"
))`

**In Exercise 2, why could the R code change `data/raw/scratch.csv` when the
deny rule refused the direct edit?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The deny rule was written with the wrong path",
  answer = "Edit rules apply to Claude Code's file-editing tools (and shell redirects), not to R code it runs",
  "R code always runs with administrator rights",
  "Deny rules only apply in plan mode"
))`

**In the demonstration, why did `here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")` get
past the guard hook?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Hooks do not run for R code",
  answer = "The guard matches the text 'data/raw', and the call never contains that text",
  "here::here() runs with administrator rights",
  "The hook was registered for the wrong event"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards
if it is useful to you.

### A guard hook

A `PreToolUse` hook receives the pending tool call as JSON on standard input
(stdin). If it exits with status 2, the call is denied and its message is
passed to the model. Claude Code and Posit Assistant use the same shape for
this, so one script can serve both.

The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code
that mentions a protected path.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ----
# PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant.
# Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call
# mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own
# guard".

protected <- c(
  "data/raw",
  "tests/fixtures",
  "make_reference.R",
  ".github/workflows"
)

payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits,
# shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields
call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE))
hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]

if (length(hits) > 0) {
  message(
    "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name,
    " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ",
    "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it."
  )
  quit(save = "no", status = 2)
}

quit(save = "no", status = 0)
```

The script runs with `Rscript --vanilla`, so it does not start renv, and
`jsonlite` must be installed in your user library.

**Register it with Claude Code** by adding a `hooks` key to
`.claude/settings.json`, alongside the existing `permissions` key. The deny
rules protect `.claude/`, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The `matcher` lists the tool names the hook runs for.

**Register it with Posit Assistant** in `.posit/assistant/settings.json`. The
tool names differ: `edit`, `bash`, and `executeR` for R code run in your
session.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Test the hook before you trust it
::::
::::{.task-container}

Hooks fail open. If the script crashes, for example because `jsonlite` is not
installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the call. So test the
script directly, without the agent, from the repository root. These commands
are for Git Bash on Windows, or the terminal on macOS or Linux; they do not
work in PowerShell.

**In the terminal:**

```bash
echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}' \
  | Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R
echo "exit status: $?"
```

Expect a message and `exit status: 2`. Then test a harmless call:

```bash
echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}' \
  | Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R
echo "exit status: $?"
```

Expect `exit status: 0`. Any other status means the hook is broken and is
silently allowing everything.

Now repeat the request from step 3 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions
`data/raw`, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt.

To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, temporarily add a `PostToolUse`
hook with no matcher that appends its input to a log file (Posit Assistant's
hooks documentation gives an example), and read the log.

::::
:::

### Break your own guard

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Red-team the tripwire
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

The guard searches for the text `data/raw`. This call never contains it, because
`here::here()` assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the
call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.

This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious
form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code's
documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a
tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall.
`git status` still catches the change. Restore the file before moving on.

::::
:::

**Your guard hook depends on jsonlite, which is not installed. What happens
when the agent tries to edit a protected file?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve it",
  answer = "The edit goes ahead: hooks fail open, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the call",
  "The agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installed",
  "The edit is blocked only in plan mode"
))`

### The review gate on GitHub

Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely, such as the
Copilot cloud agent. There, the controls are on the repository itself. Neither
file below is in the workshop template; you create them.

**1. CODEOWNERS.** Create `.github/CODEOWNERS` on your default branch:

```
/data/raw/            @your-github-username
/tests/               @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
/hooks/               @your-github-username
/.claude/             @your-github-username
/.posit/              @your-github-username
```

Code owners are requested for review automatically when a pull request changes
the files they own. CODEOWNERS works in public repositories on free plans; for
private repositories it requires a paid plan.

**2. Branch protection.** In the repository settings, add a rule for `main`
that requires a pull request before merging, requires review from code owners,
and requires the `r-checks` status check to pass. The `r-checks` workflow is
set up in the *Going further* section of
[Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd).

**3. Test it.** Open a pull request that changes a file under `tests/`, for
example by asking the Copilot cloud agent to "update the test to use a
tolerance of 1e-6". Confirm that the pull request cannot merge until you have
reviewed it.

GitHub does not let you approve your own pull request. In a repository where
you are the only person, a pull request you open yourself may need an
administrator override, which is a reason to test this gate with an agent's
pull request.

### Feedback hooks: useful, with a warning

Hooks can do more than block. A `PostToolUse` hook can run `lintr` on each R file
the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A `Stop` hook can run the test
suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is
powerful and dangerous: an agent told it cannot stop until tests pass may try
to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook protect
`tests/`.
